author: buchanan_robert
text: But how shall we make them see?

author: cushag
text:
All day they wandered, as children will who lose themselves in wood,
Or on hilltops, or among rocks—all day they roamed the woods and fields
Till evening came, and then they halted at last; but what lay before them?

They had lost their way, yet neither knew where either went. They searched

In vain for tracks that might lead them home again. The sun set, and rose

The night, when suddenly a star appeared above them out of space.

I am tired of life—of this our little world!
Why cannot I be like thee?

O my brother!

Thy spirit can soar through space sublime,

Thy soul is filled with light divine.

author: buchanan_robert
text: This is one of those poems which cannot be quoted from because every line should stand alone as an absolute unit; yet no other poem I know can better illustrate the spirit of Wordsworth. The first verse might be written by Keats or Shelley—it breathes their breath. The second is Wordsworth’s own; the rhythm is the characteristic “simple naturalness” for which the Lake Poets were always striving, but here we have this feeling of utter loss for which we look only in their poetry. And so at the end again we return to Wordsworth, and find that note of joy even in the most sorrow

author: buchanan_robert
text:
I lay down on the old leather sofa,

Where the brown dog slept before me;

author: cushag
text:
I got a wife she's quite a beauty,

And the children we have are all our own;

But if you come to my house for supper,

Don't be surprised if you find a broken hen.

author: emily_dickinson
text:
My husband, he can drink a gallon o' beer

An run up stairs on his head.

I remember Johnny an' I were married many a long time agone; an we had our share of joy and trouble. But it all passed away now—and this is the last thing that ever will happen to me! The little ones are grown up, and gone on with their lives, while the old folks have just dropped off like leaves in autumn. Only they never drop off till you think there's nothing left but skin and bone to them! So it seemed to be when poor Johnny died, as though he must always be living with us. He would do everything, even get up

author: cushag
text: I am sure that it would be very good policy in every case to allow the father or mother to look after their own children, and to keep them out of work if possible; but in many cases this cannot be done. If we had not these wretched homes which must be supported, there might be no want among our people; so long as such places are necessary we have some duty to perform.

author: cushag
text:
Little Willie came to see his gran-father
One day in January;
The doctor said he might die if
He didn't go and eat.

So he went out on the road, and picked up
a little bit o' bread ;
Then he took it home again, an' fed it to his mother.

author: emily_dickinson
john_keats
text:
I do not know what may befall,
 What sudden fate may come;
 But this I know -- there is no wealth
 The world can give me home.

My little lamb has lost his way;
 He thinks that this is green meadow land;
 But it is not, for he knows not how;
 The grass that grows upon the sand,
 Is hard as iron when the wind blows.
 It hurts him so, poor little fellow,
 To walk along with aching feet!

text:
I am a little child,
 All dressed in yellow;
 I live so far away,
 That I seldom see you,
 My eyes are very blue,

author: john_keats
text:
The long-suffering sun had warmed the air,
With gentle warmth; for not a wind did blow:
Yet never yet had there been such weather;
Nor ever should there be again so clear.

author: john_masefield

text:
But as I passed it now,
My heart grew sick at such beauty;
I stood within the door
As if they were my own!
And when those eyes beheld me,
How could I help but tell them,
In accents loud and clear—
They are my own, my own!!

Two other pieces from this collection are as follows:

On the subject of a young man who has married an old woman who is already possessed of two grown up daughters. The husband wants his own children instead of them. He says that he will leave home unless the wife consents to have more babies.

The first lines run thus:

In vain she begs him to stay,
But nothing seems to touch his heart;

author: john_masefield
text:
"They say they saw him in a pub at West Kirby,
Drinking and gambling like he couldn't care,
Telling all who asked his name that it didn't matter.
Then the other day I found out what had happened."

author: john_masefield
text:
'Now I know where my duty lies!
When the old grey head grows weaker,
I shall not turn away from it,
My life is a thing that must be given!'"

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
I have nothing here to say about her,
Nothing to add; for all things must
come out in due time.

Yet if she should ask to speak with me,
Her spirit would rise up from my breast,
And through those eyes of hers, which were
so sweet

To every heart they ever glanced upon,
Would come such a blinding light, such
a gleam,

As even that great sun of mine had never known.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
The world is an ocean, its surface a lake,

Its rivers run into it; but let them sink

In their own stream or disappear in the sea!

I will have no more of this kind of life;
God’s own ship is enough for me. . .. Oh,
you cannot understand it! No man can!

No, never a woman yet has understood. . ,

But if she had come with me now, to tell him he was so old . . .,

He would have listened to her . . .. Yes, we’re all afraid of death!

“We’ll go home,” said Sarah, in answer to my father’s wish that we should travel on together. He looked surprised; as though

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
A young man said to his grandfather:

Grandfather, why do you look so gloomy all the time?

The old man replied, “I am worried about our children.”

Why are they not as happy as we were when we were their age?

My son asked me yesterday: “What is love?”

I answered him: “If you put your hand in mine, you will understand.”

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
The “Old Woman” is all right; she’ll make
a good ship-keeper when we sail away;

But it would break my heart if any harm

Should come to her in this world below.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text: By your good will, let me die; for I have had enough of life already, since I am grown so old;

author: robert_frost

text:
Didst thou know Philip in former days, when he

was a boy; for I have heard it said that thou

wast wont to play about him and with him as a toy.

But now hast thou come unto manhood’s estate,

and art armed in the armour of battle,

with sword and spear.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
* The last lines are in allusion to the famous
sentence in Horace’s ode on liberty—

“Hic dolor est qui remanet”–the pain which is left.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
robert_frost
text:
"The very way he goes about the work
Shows how he'd do if left alone. When we are out,
His wife looks after him; she manages quite well,
For she knows all the tricks they use on men like him—-
She helps them not to make too free with her."

author: stephen_crane
text:
"Oh! you must have been happy then,-
You were so young,--you never knew
What fear and pain could mean in life;
For me they are not things unknown,
But one who cares for all that's dear
Will see them through to joy again,
And know how great is love indeed."

"Once, while I was lying sick in bed,
The man who used to tend me came to see,
And said, "You were very kind to my father.
It grieves me to think that you are troubled,
Now the world has so many people like me;
But all the same I would not desert you."
I looked up as from some evil dream—
I knew well who he meant. And then I smiled.

author: robert_frost
text:
"Here is some more from my notebook:

"'What does your friend do for a living?'
Said you: I said, "'The world has no need
Of idle people; every hand should work
To fill its quota, and the day grow short.'"
This makes them fidget in their seats. They look
At me as if they would prefer to meet
Some other man, who seems less well set.
They don't ask why I am a beggar here.
Perhaps it isn't worth while asking now.
It always hurts—this question asked so late

author: robert_frost
text:
"We want no money from you," she said;
"But we know how useful the work you do would be
To some one who does not yet exist—
One whom God shall bring in His own good time.
But you are working for yourself, not for Him.
You forget the day you were born again."

author: stephen_crane
text:
All things are possible for the child!
 For she is all hope and light;
 She has no cares or fears,
 Nor does her heart grow dark with night.
 All things are natural to the child,
 And she knows not shame or pride;
 Her simple soul grows wilder as she moves through life's strange maze.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
They had been talking for a long time
And then they looked at me.
I thought I saw them smile.
So I sang.

In this little town there once lived
 Three wise old owls.
 And they sat at the window all day long
 Watching everything outside and inside;
 But they knew not what they watched for.
 The one on the right was brown.
 Her eyes looked down on her neck.
 One eye seemed to smile with pleasure
 To see things as they happened.
 She had an owl-like beak.
 When she was about to speak,
 The two others turned their faces toward her,
 As if they waited to know what came out of it.

author: stephen_crane
stephen_crane
stothert_james_a
text:
Heard you ? — The wind has blown, a gust from over the sea,
Which shook the leaves upon their branches,—
Flicked them back with gentle breath into one another’s face,
They parted and were closed again ;

And I have heard, where there are people, some voices raised,
Some talk about him whom we loved so well;
There was not much said, but something,—something which stirred me,
Something in his name which made my heart swell :—

author: thomas_hardy
text:
Love is a fire; but Love more still ;
The light, and warmth, and music are not less :
Yet ’tis a secret flame for which I pine—
Not seen,—not heard,—unheard or unseen!

The Sun's bright disc is in my heart revealed;
But see—his rays are gone! they cannot steal,
Or hold me there,—for I am linked elsewhere :
I hear a voice, and something in the air
Pulls my soul back from sunlit realms so fair ;
To meet this power, no longer can we dwell,
Our hearts are now in other realms enthralled.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
The magnet's power lies in its own deep centre;
It never yet was found, or could be sought, without,
Save through a medium drawn therefrom. The centre


Is the soul of this great soul of Nature's heart.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
Oh! thou who bring’st me nearer and dearer —

What, through thy touch, is Life ? What this world?
This universe is Love; these words are Prayer ;
The Heavens themselves a single Soul unfold,
Like ours, in one eternal breath enfold,

author: thomas_hardy
text:
THERE was a time I did not know
 The power that love has held me!
 There came a day when Love gave voice,
 But it was long ago—I am old!

And another by the poet William Morris:

author: william_wordsworth
text:
And thou, who seekest art and fame
 In works, not words, thou shalt be blest!
 Thou wilt behold thy mind revealed
 By beauty that will live on rest;

author: thomas_hardy
text:
I am alone upon my bed,
    The twilight fading fast behind,
And all the world is hushed as dead,
   Save only one small bird that sings!

author: thomas_hardy
text:
I stand and stare, with wistful eyes,
 While I look down on that old world lies.
 Onward and ever my feet go:
 To me its future looks slow.

author: william_wordsworth
buchanan_robert
text: “The great men of our country, whose minds have been exalted, and whom we all look up to, are now in their last struggles for fame, and will soon pass away from us. But thou art still young, sweet nightingale, though thy voice is harsh and shrill; the days may come when thou shalt sing with softer notes than those which now disturb thy fellow-birds.”

I know a star whose constant light
 Is kept from all but me,
 Whose beam upon this midnight night
 Can never reach its tree.

It hangs above me in the sky,
 It shines across my bed,
 And every time it seems to fly
 So near, so near indeed.

Now wherefore, oh, why cannot I
 To kiss that light divine?
 My hands are tied, my soul denied
 A vision like his mine.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
Where now, oh where, are those who thought us free?
 Where those who call us Englishmen, our countrymen,
 To whom we did their hearts and souls extend,
 The better portion which in man was given them,
 They, who our very thoughts embraced so kindly?
 Oh were they not all gone like some old men,
 Their youth being consumed, or like old women,
 Who through the world have brought forth every child,
 And now have no more strength to bear new fruit?
 Nor has this age been less than any other.

author: william_wordsworth

On hearing that Napoleon had been defeated at Waterloo, in 1815.


The conqueror sleeps beneath his tents—the sun

 Of better times, when from the ruined man
